ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In a certain space, there exists a uniform magnetic field in the vertical direction (not shown). Two parallel metal rails, afe and bcd, are placed within this field, with the cdef portion of the rails lying in the horizontal plane. When adjusting the inclination angle $\theta$ of the inclined plane abcf, it is observed that a metal rod of length $l = 0.2\,\mathrm{m}$ can remain stationary on the rails only when $\theta$ is between $37^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. It is known that the distance between the rails is $l = 0.2\,\mathrm{m}$, and a power source with an electromotive force $E = 15\,\mathrm{V}$ is connected between points e and d. The mass of the metal rod is $0.1\,\mathrm{kg}$, the internal resistance of the power source $r$ and the resistance of the metal rod $R$ are both $1\,\Omega$, the resistance of the rails and wires can be neglected, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the metal rod and the rails is $\mu$ (unknown), with the maximum static friction equal to the kinetic friction. $\sin37^{\circ} = 0.6$, $\cos37^{\circ} = 0.8$, and $g$ is taken as $10\,\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. What is the magnetic induction intensity $B$?
2. When $\theta=53^{\circ}$, if the power supply is replaced with a switch and the switch is initially open, causing the metal rod to slide down from a height of $h{=}0.72\mathrm{m}$ above the horizontal plane where cdef is located, what is the magnitude of the velocity $v$ of the metal rod when it reaches $c f$?
3. Under the condition of sub_question_2, what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the metal rod when the switch is suddenly closed? (The metal rod only changes the direction of its velocity, not the magnitude, when passing through cf.)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure two parallel metal guide rails can be seen, the left guide rail passes through a, f, e, and the right guide rail passes through b, c, d; ab is a metal rod placed on the inclined plane abcf and spanning the two guide rails, and near cf dashed lines indicate the boundary between the inclined plane and the lower horizontal part cdef. Between e and d in the lower left there is a power supply symbol connected, marked with E and internal resistance r; beside point c the angle θ between the inclined plane and the horizontal plane is marked. The magnetic field is not drawn in the figure; the problem statement says it is in the vertical direction. Then reason: when the power supply is connected, the total resistance of the circuit is R+r=1+1=2 Ω, and the current I=E/(R+r)=15/2=7.5 A. Let the magnitude of the Ampere force on the metal rod be F=BIl. According to the angle range in which it can be stationary given by the problem as 37° to 90°, and according to the geometric relationship in the figure that the rod spans the guide rails and the inclined plane abcf is tilted, decompose the Ampere force into the inclined-plane direction and the normal direction; choose the magnetic field direction so that the Ampere force has an upward component along the inclined plane, then the component of the Ampere force along the inclined plane is F cosθ, the downward component of gravity along the inclined plane is mg sinθ, and the support force N=mg cosθ+F sinθ. The stationary condition is |F cosθ-mg sinθ|≤μN. The endpoints of the allowed angle interval correspond to the maximum static friction reaching the limit. When θ=90°, cos90°=0, sin90°=1, there is mg=μF. Given m=0.1 kg, g=10 m/s², so mg=1 N, therefore μ=1/F. When θ=37°, take the lower-endpoint limit: F cos37°−mg sin37°=μ(mg cos37°+F sin37°). Substitute sin37°=0.6, cos37°=0.8, mg=1, μ=1/F, obtaining 0.8F−0.6=(1/F)(0.8+0.6F)=0.8/F+0.6. Rearranging gives 0.8F−1.2=0.8/F, namely 0.8F²−1.2F−0.8=0, solving gives F=2 N (discard the negative root). Therefore μ=mg/F=1/2=0.5. Thus B=F/(Il)=2/(7.5×0.2)=2/1.5=4/3 T. From the previous choice of Ampere force direction and the relationship of current direction, the magnetic field direction is vertically downward. Second question: when θ=53°, sin53°=cos37°=0.8, cos53°=sin37°=0.6. When the switch is open there is no current and no Ampere force. The rod slides from a height h=0.72 m above the horizontal plane to cf, and the displacement along the inclined plane s=h/sin53°=0.72/0.8=0.9 m. Use the work-energy theorem: mgh−μmg cos53°·s=mv²/2. Substitute μ=0.5, g=10, cos53°=0.6, s=0.9, obtaining v²=2g(sin53°−μcos53°)s=20×(0.8−0.5×0.6)×0.9=9, so v=3 m/s. Third question: after the rod passes cf, the speed magnitude does not change, and when entering the horizontal part v=3 m/s. After the switch is suddenly closed, the moving conducting rod cuts the vertical magnetic field and produces a motional electromotive force ε=Blv=(4/3)×0.2×3=0.8 V. According to the specified method, take the total circuit resistance R+r=2 Ω, then the induced current I'=ε/(R+r)=0.8/2=0.4 A. The magnitude of the magnetic resistance force F_B=BI'l=(4/3)×0.4×0.2=0.1067 N. On the horizontal plane the support force equals mg, and the magnitude of the friction force f=μmg=0.5×1=0.5 N. Both hinder the motion, so the magnitude of the acceleration a=(f+F_B)/m=(0.5+0.1067)/0.1≈6.07 m/s².
